A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SonicMaster work. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V2 reports original restoration experiments, architecture and conditioning ablations, historical-piano evaluations, listening studies and appendix solver experiments.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, shuffled-prompt results and updated listening-study outcomes.

M1.justification: The VAE, FLAN-T5 conditioning, MM-DiT/DiT architecture, rectified-flow objective, Euler inference and overlapping-segment procedure remain unchanged. V3's main-table SonicMaster model matches v2's Large variant; added baseline procedures do not modify SonicMaster.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluation on RemFX clean/effected test pairs for dynamics and reverb, and tests mismatched instructions through prompt shuffling. The Jamendo-derived training/evaluation coverage, nineteen degradation types, full-song evaluation and historical-piano recordings remain.

E2.justification: V3 adds Text2FX-directional to objective EQ and comparative listening evaluations, while retaining the former Text2FX-EQ baseline as Text2FXcos. Section 5.1 and Figure 3 additionally compare against DPTNet, UMX, DCUNet, TCN and HDemucs under the RemFX protocol, substantially broadening the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Listening-study participation increases from 8 to 12 and from 13 to 20. V3 introduces RemFX evaluation using SI-SDR and describes effect-specific baseline training with L1 plus multi-resolution STFT losses; it also introduces directional-baseline and prompt-shuffling procedures. Section 4.1 revises spectral balance from eight to nine bands, without establishing that retained scores were recomputed.

E4.justification: V3 adds one targeted controllability test: shuffling test-set prompts and comparing against correct and absent prompts. Existing solver, model-size, audio-conditioning and long-form analyses remain; their relocation and consolidation in Appendix A.7 do not constitute new ablations. The spectrogram examples are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions already report listening-study 95% confidence intervals and paired t-tests. V3 additionally reports numerical significance bounds: p < 0.05 for Stereo and p < 0.01 for the other significant categories. No model-seed or repeated-training-run reporting change is documented.

E6.justification: V3 adds directional-baseline, shuffled-prompt and RemFX results, including SonicMaster SI-SDR of 47.11/45.76 dB for dynamics/reverb. Listening MOS values change, and Dynamics becomes statistically significant. Comparative preferences change from 128/130 to 191/200 for reverb and 122/130 to 180/200 for EQ; changed participation and EQ comparators prevent treating these as same-setting performance changes. Figure 5 reports nine Mel2Mel reverb votes, although the prose still says two. Retained objective and appendix ablation scores otherwise remain unchanged apart from rounding.

T1.justification: The spectral-balance metric changes from an eight-band description to an explicitly defined nine-component profile in v3 Section 4.1 and Appendix A.5. Appendix A.3 also formulates the added directional baseline's loss. SonicMaster's flow equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: unified text-guided restoration/mastering for nineteen degradations, automatic operation, the paired text-conditioned dataset and strong restoration performance. The added experiments support existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V3 distinguishes intentional mastering from minimal-alteration effect removal, explains weaker EQ listening responses through stylistic or subtle effects, and suggests an unfavorable MM-DiT/DiT ratio explains the weaker 6/6 variant. The limitations concerning latent artifacts, segment joining and reverberation assessment in Section 6 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New appendices substantially expand reproducibility information: directional-baseline optimization, initialization, circular shifts and contrast-prompt construction; metric frequency boundaries, STFT parameters and modulation-spectrum code. V3 also adds a statement promising training, inference and evaluation code plus dataset release upon acceptance. This documents intended access, rather than proving a resource became available.

R1.justification: V3 adds InstructME, RemFX and references supporting the newly compared removal architectures. It explains how text-conditioned mastering differs from effect removal and why directional Text2FX is relevant. These are focused extensions within the retained related-work framework and novelty positioning.

P1.justification: V3 makes localized wording, citation-style and contact-text edits, expands explanations and reorganizes some ablation discussion and appendix sections. Most existing prose, including the abstract, architecture description, discussion and conclusion, remains essentially unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 substantially restructures Tables 1–3, moving model-size and audio-conditioning rows into expanded appendix Tables 8–10. V2's listening Tables 5–6 become v3's bar-chart Figures 4–5, and a new SI-SDR comparison appears as Figure 3. Existing diagrams and spectrograms are retained or relocated, with some caption revisions.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens the empirical case through a shuffled-prompt control, broader evaluated baselines and larger listening samples, while Appendix A.5 makes evaluation more reproducible. These provide a net improvement, tempered by reporting errors: Table 1 mislabels the ablation block as full-song evaluation, and Section 5.4 contradicts Figure 5's Mel2Mel reverb vote count. The gains therefore support a limited rather than substantial overall quality improvement.
